docs.title: Dev Best Practices
docs.text: Short, practical notes on how we build software: patterns that work, pitfalls we hit, and settings worth copying.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Backend: Django, ORM, APIs, background tasks.
  • Frontend: UI frameworks, tooling, performance.
  • GitHub: account setup, repositories, Actions.
  • Security: secrets, access, dependencies.

Want to add a note? See Contributing.

docs.title: Where to put a note
docs.text:
One topic per file, inside the section it belongs to:

docs/
├── backend/
│   └── django/
│       └── orm-n-plus-one.md
├── frontend/
├── github/
└── security/
  • File names are lowercase and hyphen-separated: orm-n-plus-one.md.
  • A new folder needs an index.md that says what the folder covers.
  • The site menu is built from the folder tree, so you do not edit mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Note template
docs.text:
# <Title: what to do, e.g. "Use select_related for foreign keys">

**TL;DR:** one or two sentences with the rule.

## Problem

What goes wrong without it. Show the bad code or setting.

## Solution

```python
# the good version
```

## Why it works

Short explanation. Link to official docs.

## Trade-offs

Skip this section when there is only one sane way.

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| A      |      |      |
| B      |      |      |

!!! tip "Recommendation"
    Which option to pick and when.

## Pitfalls

!!! warning
    Cases where the rule does not apply.

docs.title: GitHub

Account and repository setup, branch protection, pull requests, GitHub Actions.

  • Privacy: commit email, profile, and other places that expose personal data.
  • Repository settings: protect main, pull request rules, security features, GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
What GitHub shows about you to anyone on the internet, and how to limit it.

TL;DR: commit with the GitHub no-reply email, hide the email on your profile, and don't rewrite old public history just to remove an email: it is already copied elsewhere.

docs.title: Why bother
docs.text:
Public GitHub data is scraped all the time. A real email or name in a commit leads to:

  • spam and recruiter mailing lists;
  • targeted phishing ("your repo X has a security issue, log in here");
  • linking your GitHub identity to your other accounts.

Whatever is in a public commit stays public forever: forks, clones, GH Archive and Software Heritage keep copies you cannot delete.

docs.title: What GitHub exposes
docs.text: Data Where anyone can see it How to limit it Commit email git log, <commit URL>.patch Commit email Commit name git log, GitHub UI Commit email Profile email, name, location, company Your profile page Profile Activity: when and how much you work Contribution graph, activity feed Profile Time zone Commit timestamps, profile local time Other leaks Public SSH and GPG keys github.com/<user>.keys, github.com/<user>.gpg Other leaks Email in published packages PyPI, npm metadata Other leaks

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Settings → Emails: Keep my email addresses private is on.
  • Settings → Emails: Block command line pushes that expose my email is on.
  • git config --global user.email is your no-reply address.
  • Settings → Public profile: Public email is "Don't show my email address".
  • Your GPG key, if any, has no personal email in it.
  • pyproject.toml / package.json of published packages have no personal email.

docs.title: Hide your email in commits
docs.text: TL;DR: set user.email to your GitHub no-reply address and turn on both email privacy settings. Leave old public history as it is unless nobody has cloned the repo yet.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Git writes the author email into every commit. On GitHub anyone can read it, even when the web UI shows only your username:

git clone https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git && git log --format='%an <%ae>'
curl -s https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<sha>.patch | head -3

This also applies to private repositories: everyone with access sees the email, and it becomes public the day the repo is made public.

docs.title: 1. Find your no-reply address
docs.text:
Settings → Emails, under Keep my email addresses private. Or:

gh api user --jq '"\(.id)+\(.login)@users.noreply.github.com"'

Accounts created after July 18, 2017 get the ID+USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com form. Older accounts may have USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com.

Use the ID-based form

Commits with the old USERNAME@ form stop linking to your account if you rename it. The ID-based form survives a rename. To get it, turn Keep my email addresses private off and on again.

docs.title: 2. Turn on both settings
docs.text:
Settings → Emails:

  • Keep my email addresses private: commits made in the web UI (merging a PR, editing a file) use the no-reply address.
  • Block command line pushes that expose my email: GitHub rejects a push if a commit contains your private email, with GH007: Your push would publish a private email address. This catches a misconfigured machine before the email goes public.

docs.title: 3. Set the email in Git
docs.text:
git config --global user.email "12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com"

Check the last commit:

git log -1 --format='%an <%ae>'

docs.title: Which email to use
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons GitHub no-reply Nothing to harvest. Commits still count on your profile. Nobody can email you from git log. Links only to GitHub, not GitLab or others. Public alias (dev@yourdomain.com) People can contact you. You can filter or drop it later. Still harvested, so expect spam. You need a domain or alias service. Plus address (me+github@gmail.com) Easy to filter. Bots strip +github and get your real address. Real personal email No setup. Spam and phishing, permanently.

Recommendation

No-reply for GitHub. Use a real address only where the workflow needs it, for example patches sent by email to a mailing list.

docs.title: Work and personal identities
docs.text:
One global email is wrong as soon as you have work repos. Two ways to switch it:

By folderBy remote URLNo default at all 
# ~/.gitconfig
[user]
    name = Your Name
    email = 12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com

# /i = case-insensitive, needed on Windows
[includeIf "gitdir/i:~/work/"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-work

# ~/.gitconfig-work
[user]
    email = you@company.com

Pros: simple. Cons: a work repo cloned outside ~/work/ gets the personal email.

# ~/.gitconfig, needs Git 2.36+
[includeIf "hasconfig:remote.*.url:git@github.com:my-company/**"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-work

Pros: works wherever the repo lives. Cons: does not apply before origin is added, so the very first commit of a new repo can get the wrong email.

git config --global --unset user.email
git config --global user.useConfigOnly true

Git refuses to commit until you set user.email in the repo. Pros: never the wrong identity. Cons: one extra command in every new repo.

docs.title: Name
docs.text: user.name is just as public. A real name helps employers and colleagues find your work. A handle keeps your GitHub separate from your real identity. Pick one on purpose.

docs.title: Old commits
docs.text: Changing the settings affects only new commits. Old ones keep the old email.

docs.title: Leave them
docs.text:
• Pros: nothing breaks.
  • Cons: the email stays in history.

For a public repo this is usually the right call: forks, clones and archives already have the old commits, so a rewrite does not un-publish the email.

docs.title: Rewrite them
docs.text:
# mailmap.txt: new identity, then old email
Your Name <12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com> <old@example.com>

git filter-repo --mailmap mailmap.txt
git remote add origin git@github.com:<owner>/<repo>.git  # filter-repo removes origin on purpose
git push --force --all && git push --force --tags
  • Pros: the email is gone from the repo's current branches.
  • Cons: every commit SHA changes. Clones, forks and open PRs break. Commit signatures are lost. Old commits stay reachable by SHA on GitHub until GitHub Support purges them, and forks keep them anyway.

When a rewrite is worth it

A private repo you are about to make public, or a repo nobody else has cloned.

.mailmap is not a fix

A .mailmap file in the repo only changes what git log and git shortlog print. The commits still contain the old email.

docs.title: Other leaks
docs.text: Places that expose personal data even after you fixed your commit email and profile.

docs.title: Public SSH and GPG keys
docs.text:
Anyone can download the public keys of any GitHub user:

curl https://github.com/<user>.keys
curl https://github.com/<user>.gpg

GPG: a GPG key contains its user IDs, so <user>.gpg shows every email in the key. If you sign commits with GPG and use the no-reply address, create the key with the no-reply address only.

SSH: a public key is safe to share, but the same key on many servers links your accounts together. A server can check which of your GitHub keys you offer when you connect.

Option Pros Cons One SSH key everywhere Simple. Your GitHub account can be linked to every other server you use. One key per service Nothing to link. More keys to manage and rotate.

With separate keys, stop SSH from offering every key to every server:

# ~/.ssh/config
Host github.com
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_github
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Tip

Signing commits with an SSH key instead of GPG avoids putting an email into a key at all.

docs.title: Time zone in commits
docs.text:
Every commit stores the UTC offset of your machine, for example +0200. Together with the commit times this shows your region and working hours.

Committing in UTC hides the offset:

TZ=UTC git commit
  • Pros: the offset no longer points to your region.
  • Cons: local git log shows UTC. Commit times still show when you work.

Most people accept the offset. Bother only if your location really must stay secret.

docs.title: Package metadata
docs.text:
Publishing a package copies its metadata to PyPI or npm, where it stays even after you delete the package:

# pyproject.toml
authors = [{ name = "Your Name", email = "you@personal.com" }]  # public forever

Use a project address or the no-reply address, or leave email out.

docs.title: Secret gists are not private
docs.text: A secret gist is only unlisted. Anyone with the URL can open it, and the URL leaks through browser history, chat previews and logs. Use a private repository for anything sensitive.

docs.title: Logs and screenshots in issues
docs.text:
Stack traces and terminal output often contain your OS username, machine name, internal hostnames or tokens:

File "C:\Users\john.smith\work\acme-billing\app.py", line 42

Read pasted output before posting, and crop screenshots.

docs.title: Profile and activity
docs.text: TL;DR: hide the public email, fill in only the profile fields you want strangers to see, and decide on purpose whether your activity is visible.

docs.title: Profile fields
docs.text:
Settings → Public profile. Every field here is public and indexed by search engines.

Field Recommendation Public email "Don't show my email address". People who need to reach you can open an issue. Name Real name if GitHub is part of your professional profile, otherwise a handle. Location Country or city at most. Company, social links Only if you want them connected to this account. Local time Shows your time zone. Leave it off unless you want people to know when you are online.

docs.title: Private contributions
docs.text:
Profile → Contribution settings above the contribution graph → Private contributions.

The graph then also counts commits to private repos. Repo names stay hidden.

  • Pros: the graph reflects your real work, useful when most of it is in private repos.
  • Cons: shows when and how much you work: weekends, holidays, gaps.

docs.title: Private profile
docs.text:
Settings → Public profile → Contributions & Activity → Make profile private and hide activity.

Hides the contribution graph, activity feed, achievements, follower counts, organizations, stars and the sponsor button. Keeps visible the README, bio and avatar.

  • Pros: strangers cannot track your activity from one page.
  • Cons: you cannot receive GitHub Sponsors. Your commits, issues and comments in public repos stay visible there, and some data is still reachable through the API. It does not hide what happened before you turned it on.

Note

A private profile hides the overview, not the work. Anyone can still find your public commits and comments repo by repo.

docs.title: Repository settings
docs.text:
How to set up a GitHub repository so that main is protected, every change goes through a PR, and the repo does not leak secrets or run untrusted code.

TL;DR: a ruleset on main that blocks deletion, force pushes and direct pushes, and requires CI; squash merging only; every security feature under Advanced Security on; a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and actions pinned to a commit SHA.

The advice is for a solo or personal repo first. Where a team needs something different (review approvals, CODEOWNERS), the page says so.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page Covers Protect the main branch Rulesets vs branch protection, blocking direct and force pushes, required PRs and CI, bypass list, tags. Pull request settings Merge methods, auto-merge, deleting merged branches. Security features Dependabot, secret scanning, push protection, code scanning, vulnerability reporting. GitHub Actions settings GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, pinning actions, fork PRs, deploy secrets.

docs.title: What your plan allows
docs.text: Feature Public repo, any plan Private repo, Free Private repo, Pro / Team Rulesets and branch protection yes no yes Dependabot alerts and updates yes yes yes Secret scanning, push protection, code scanning yes, free no Team or Enterprise organization with GitHub Secret Protection / Code Security Private vulnerability reporting yes no no

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
Protect main (details):

  • Branch ruleset main targets the default branch, Enforcement status is Active.
  • Restrict deletions and Block force pushes are on.
  • Require a pull request before merging is on. Required approvals: 0 solo, 1+ team.
  • Require status checks to pass before merging lists the CI job.
  • Bypass list is empty, or holds only the bot that really needs to push.
  • A tag ruleset protects v* tags from updates and deletion.

Pull requests (details):

  • Only Allow squash merging is on, with Pull request title and description.
  • Automatically delete head branches is on.
  • Always suggest updating pull request branches and Allow auto-merge are on.

Security (details):

  • Dependabot alerts and Dependabot security updates are on.
  • .github/dependabot.yml updates at least github-actions.
  • Secret scanning and Push protection are on.
  • Code scanning: CodeQL analysis uses the Default setup.
  • Private vulnerability reporting is on and SECURITY.md says how to report.

Actions (details):

  • Workflow permissions is Read repository contents and packages permissions.
  • Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests is off.
  • Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
  • Fork PR workflows need approval from a maintainer.
  • Deploy secrets live in an environment, not in repository secrets.

docs.title: GitHub Actions settings
docs.text: TL;DR: make GITHUB_TOKEN read-only by default and grant write per job in the workflow, don't let Actions approve PRs, pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, and require approval before running workflows from fork PRs.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A workflow runs code you did not write (every uses: line) with a token that can push to the repo. The defaults on older repos make this worse:

  • GITHUB_TOKEN gets read and write access to everything, in every job;
  • uses: some/action@v3 runs whatever commit the v3 tag points to today. Whoever controls that action can move the tag;
  • a workflow can approve a PR, which defeats the review rule in the main ruleset.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Settings → Actions → General:

Setting Value Actions permissions Allow OWNER, and select non-OWNER, actions and reusable workflows, with Allow actions created by GitHub on and your list of allowed actions Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA on Approval for running fork pull request workflows from contributors Require approval for first-time contributors or stricter Workflow permissions Read repository contents and packages permissions Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests off

Then give each job only what it needs in the workflow file:

permissions: {}            # workflow default: no access at all

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-length SHA>  # v4.2.2
      - run: make build

  deploy:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write      # only this job can push
    steps:
      - ...

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
• The token setting is the default for every workflow. The permissions: key in YAML overrides it, so a job gets write access only where the file says so, and a reviewer sees it in the diff.
  • A commit SHA cannot be moved. If the action's repo is taken over, you keep running the code you checked.
  • Fork PRs are where untrusted code comes from. Approval means a maintainer looks at the PR before it runs on your runners.

See Security hardening for GitHub Actions and Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository.

docs.title: Pin actions to a commit SHA
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons Major tag (@v4) Gets fixes automatically. Easy to read. The tag can be moved to malicious code, and you run it on the next workflow run. Exact tag (@v4.2.2) Easy to read. A tag is still just a pointer and can be moved. Full commit SHA (@11bd719... # v4.2.2) Immutable: you run exactly the code you reviewed. Unreadable without the comment. Never updates by itself, so you need Dependabot.

Recommendation

SHA with the version as a comment, and the github-actions ecosystem in Dependabot version updates: it bumps the SHA and the comment together. Actions from actions/* and github/* are lower risk, but the setting Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA applies to them too.

docs.title: Who can run workflows from forks
docs.text:
Public repos only. Private repos have a separate set of fork options, all off by default.

Option Pros Cons Require approval for first-time contributors who are new to GitHub Least friction for contributors. Only stops brand-new accounts. Require approval for first-time contributors One look at each new contributor's first PR. After one merged PR, a contributor's later PRs run without approval. Require approval for all external contributors Every fork PR is looked at before it runs. Maintainer has to click Approve and run on every PR from a non-collaborator.

Recommendation

Require approval for first-time contributors for a typical public repo. Require approval for all external contributors if workflows use self-hosted runners or anything expensive.

docs.title: Deploy secrets
docs.text:
• Put deploy secrets into an environment (Settings → Environments), not into repository secrets. An environment can require a reviewer and allow only certain branches, for example only main.
  • For cloud deploys, use OpenID Connect (OIDC): the cloud trusts a short-lived token from GitHub, so there is no long-lived key to leak.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
pull_request_target

It runs in the context of the base repo, with secrets and a write token, even for a fork PR. Never check out and run the PR's code in it. For a workflow that needs both untrusted code and secrets, split it into a pull_request workflow and a workflow_run one.

Switching the token to read-only breaks workflows

Workflows that push, comment, or create releases fail with 403 until their jobs declare the permissions: they need. Add the permissions: blocks first, then change the setting.

Workflow-level permissions: apply to every trigger

A contents: write at the top of a file that also runs on pull_request gives write access to runs for PRs from branches in the same repo too (fork PRs always get a read-only token). Put write permissions on the job that pushes, and keep that job behind if: github.event_name == 'push'.

docs.title: Protect the main branch
docs.text: TL;DR: add a branch ruleset for the default branch with Restrict deletions, Block force pushes, Require a pull request before merging and Require status checks to pass before merging. Leave the bypass list empty.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Out of the box, anyone with write access to the repository can:

  • push straight to main, skipping review and CI;
  • git push --force and rewrite or drop history that others have already pulled;
  • delete main by mistake.

On a repo where merging to main deploys (like this site), every one of these ships to production.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset.

  1. Ruleset name: main.
  2. Enforcement status: Active.
  3. Target branches: Add target → Include default branch.
  4. Bypass list: leave empty (see Bypass list).
  5. Rules:
Rule What it stops Restrict deletions Deleting main. Block force pushes git push --force to main. Require a pull request before merging Any direct push. Every change has to arrive through a PR. Require status checks to pass before merging Merging a PR whose CI is red or still running. Require linear history Merge commits on main. Optional, see Pull request settings.

With Require a pull request before merging on, a direct push is rejected:

remote: error: GH013: Repository rule violations found for refs/heads/main.
remote: - Changes must be made through a pull request.

docs.title: Pull request options
docs.text:
These sit under Require a pull request before merging. The right values depend on whether anyone else can review your PRs.

SoloTeam
  • Required approvals: 0. GitHub never lets you approve your own PR, so 1 would block every merge.
  • Leave the other review options off.

The PR still earns its keep: CI runs before the merge, and the diff gets one last look.

  • Required approvals: 1 or more.
  • Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed: on. An approval covers the code that was reviewed, not what was pushed later.
  • Require approval of the most recent reviewable push: on. Stops the author from pushing a change after the last approval and merging it alone.
  • Require review from Code Owners: on, together with a .github/CODEOWNERS file.
  • Require conversation resolution before merging: on, so review comments are not lost.
# .github/CODEOWNERS: the last matching pattern wins
*                    @my-org/maintainers
/docs/security/      @my-org/security
.github/workflows/   @my-org/platform

docs.title: Status checks
docs.text:
Under Require status checks to pass before merging, Add checks and pick the CI job by name. For this repo it is docs, the job in .github/workflows/deploy.yml that runs mkdocs build --strict. GitHub lists a check only after it has run at least once, so open a PR first.

Require branches to be up to date before merging makes the PR re-run CI on top of the latest main.

Option Pros Cons Up to date: on CI tested exactly what lands on main. Every merge to main makes the other open PRs update and re-run CI. Up to date: off No extra rebases or CI runs. Two PRs that pass alone can break main together.

Recommendation

On for a solo or small repo: few PRs are open at once, so the cost is low. For a busy repo, look at a merge queue (rule Require merge queue) instead of making everyone rebase.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
Rules are checked on GitHub's side, on every push and every merge, whatever client is used. A local pre-push hook can be skipped with --no-verify. A ruleset cannot.

See About rulesets and Available rules for rulesets.

docs.title: Rulesets or classic branch protection
docs.text:
GitHub has two features for this. Both are still supported and both can apply to the same branch.

Option Pros Cons Rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets) Several rulesets can stack on one branch, the strictest rule wins. Can be switched off without deleting. Anyone with read access can see them. Export to JSON and import into another repo. Also cover tags. Fewer guides online still show this UI. Branch protection rules (Settings → Branches) Older, so most tutorials use it. One rule per branch. Admins are exempt unless you turn on Do not allow bypassing the above settings. Branches only. Only admins can see the rules.

Recommendation

Rulesets for anything new. If a repo already has a branch protection rule, either convert it or keep it: GitHub enforces both, so you do not lose protection while you move.

docs.title: Bypass list
docs.text:
Whoever is on the bypass list skips every rule in the ruleset.

Option Pros Cons Empty The rules apply to everyone, you included. No "just this once" pushes to main. An emergency fix also has to go through a PR. To get around it, an admin has to switch the ruleset to Disabled, which leaves a trace. Repository admin, Always allow Hotfix without waiting for CI. Your own mistakes are no longer caught: it is too easy to push to main from the wrong terminal. Repository admin, For pull requests only Admin can merge a PR that is not approved or whose checks are red, but direct pushes are still blocked. An unreviewed merge is still one click away. A GitHub App or deploy key A release bot can push version bumps or tags. Whoever controls that token can push to main too.

Recommendation

Empty. If a bot needs to push, add only that app, and only to the ruleset it needs.

docs.title: Signed commits
docs.text:
Require signed commits accepts only commits with a verified GPG, SSH or S/MIME signature.

Option Pros Cons Off Nothing to set up. Anyone who has set user.email to your address can commit "as you". Write access is still needed to push. On Every commit on main is tied to a key on a GitHub account. Everyone, and every bot, has to sign. Unsigned commits in a PR branch can block a squash merge even though GitHub signs the squash commit itself. Merging locally needs the result signed before the push.

Recommendation

Off for a solo repo, on when several people or bots push and a forged author would matter. Sign your own commits either way, it costs one-time setup.

docs.title: Protect release tags too
docs.text: A tag like v1.2.0 can be deleted and pointed at another commit, and package managers and GitHub Actions users follow tags. Add a second ruleset: New ruleset → New tag ruleset, target v*, with Restrict updates and Restrict deletions. Add Restrict creations if only a release workflow should create tags.

docs.title: Same rules on many repos
docs.text:
A ruleset can be exported to JSON from its page and imported into another repo with New ruleset → Import a ruleset. The same JSON works with the API:

gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/rulesets                         # list
gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/rulesets --method POST --input main.json

{
  "name": "main",
  "target": "branch",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "bypass_actors": [],
  "conditions": { "ref_name": { "include": ["~DEFAULT_BRANCH"], "exclude": [] } },
  "rules": [
    { "type": "deletion" },
    { "type": "non_fast_forward" },
    { "type": "pull_request", "parameters": {
        "required_approving_review_count": 0,
        "dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push": false,
        "require_code_owner_review": false,
        "require_last_push_approval": false,
        "required_review_thread_resolution": false } },
    { "type": "required_status_checks", "parameters": {
        "strict_required_status_checks_policy": true,
        "required_status_checks": [{ "context": "docs" }] } }
  ]
}

deletion is Restrict deletions and non_fast_forward is Block force pushes. GitHub's ruleset-recipes repo has more examples.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Private repos on GitHub Free

Rulesets and branch protection work on public repos on every plan, but on private repos only with GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise. On a free private repo you can still create a ruleset, but GitHub saves it without enforcing it.

A required check that never runs

If the required check's workflow skips a PR (a paths: filter, a renamed job), the check stays "Expected" forever and the PR cannot be merged. Name the job, not the workflow, and keep the name stable.

Evaluate mode

Evaluate (dry-run: log what would be blocked) is GitHub Enterprise only. On other plans, test a new ruleset on a throwaway branch pattern before targeting main.

docs.title: Pull request settings
docs.text: TL;DR: allow squash merging only, with Pull request title and description as the commit message. Turn on Automatically delete head branches and Always suggest updating pull request branches.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: By default a repo allows all three merge methods. Each person picks a different one, so main ends up with a mix of merge commits, squashed commits and rebased WIP commits like fix typo. Merged branches pile up in the branch list.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Settings → General → Pull Requests:

Setting Value Allow merge commits off Allow squash merging on, default message Pull request title and description Allow rebase merging off Always suggest updating pull request branches on Allow auto-merge on Automatically delete head branches on

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
• One merge method means one shape of history, and nobody has to choose.
  • Pull request title and description puts the reviewed summary into the commit, instead of a list of commit messages nobody reviewed.
  • Always suggest updating pull request branches shows an Update branch button whenever the PR is behind main, so you do not have to merge main in by hand.
  • Allow auto-merge adds Enable auto-merge to a PR: it merges itself once the required reviews and checks from the ruleset pass. It has no effect without such rules.
  • Automatically delete head branches deletes the PR branch after merging. A deleted branch can be restored from the closed PR.

See About merge methods on GitHub.

docs.title: Merge methods
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons Squash One commit per PR on main: easy to read, revert and bisect. WIP commits in the branch don't matter. The individual branch commits are not on main. Branches stacked on the PR branch need a rebase after the merge. Merge commit Keeps every commit and shows where the branch joined. Works with stacked branches. main gets every fix typo commit plus a merge commit per PR. git log is hard to read without --first-parent. Rebase Linear history and every commit kept. Only good if every commit in the PR is clean. Commits are rewritten, so their SHAs change and the author's signatures are lost.

Recommendation

Squash only for most repos. A PR is the unit of review, so it is also the unit on main. Allow merge commits too only if you keep long-lived branches (for example release/*) that must be merged back without being flattened.

If you allow squash or rebase only, you can also turn on Require linear history in the main ruleset, so a merge commit cannot get in from the command line.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Squash and long-lived branches

After a squash merge, the branch's own commits are not ancestors of main. Keep working on the same branch and the next PR shows the old changes again. Start a new branch from main after each merge.

Auto-delete and forks

For a PR from a fork, GitHub checks the fork's setting, not yours. Branches with a ruleset that has Restrict deletions are not deleted either.

docs.title: Security features
docs.text: TL;DR: on a public repo, turn on everything under Settings → Advanced Security: Dependabot alerts and security updates, secret scanning with push protection, CodeQL default setup, and private vulnerability reporting. It is free for public repos.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A repo is attacked through what it already contains:

  • a dependency with a known CVE that nobody noticed;
  • an API key committed "just for a test";
  • a vulnerability that a stranger finds, and then reports in a public issue because there is no private way to report it.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Settings → Advanced Security:

Setting What it does Dependabot alerts Alerts when a dependency in your lockfile or manifest has a known vulnerability. Dependabot security updates Opens a PR that bumps the vulnerable dependency to the fixed version. Dependabot version updates Opens PRs for all new versions, on a schedule. Configured in .github/dependabot.yml, see below. Secret scanning Finds committed tokens and keys from known providers and alerts you. Many providers revoke a leaked token automatically. Push protection Rejects a push that contains a detected secret, before it is in history. CodeQL analysis → Set up → Default Code scanning: static analysis on every PR and push, results in the Security tab. Private vulnerability reporting Adds a Report a vulnerability button to the Security tab, so a reporter can open a private advisory.

Then add a SECURITY.md in the repo root or in .github/. It shows up in the Security tab:

# Security policy

Please report vulnerabilities privately with
**Security → Report a vulnerability** on this repository, not in a public issue.
We reply within 7 days.

docs.title: Dependabot version updates
docs.text:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
  - package-ecosystem: "uv"   # or pip, npm, docker...
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    groups:
      all:
        patterns: ["*"]     # one PR for all updates instead of one per package

The github-actions entry also keeps actions pinned to a commit SHA up to date, see Pin actions to a commit SHA.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
Each feature catches a problem at a different point:

  • push protection: before the secret is in history;
  • code scanning and the required status checks: before the PR is merged;
  • Dependabot: after the merge, when a new CVE is published for code you already ship;
  • private reporting: when someone else finds what all of the above missed.

See Quickstart for securing your repository and About push protection.

docs.title: Dependabot version updates
docs.text:
Security updates fix known CVEs only. Version updates bump everything, which is a different trade:

Option Pros Cons Security updates only Few PRs, each fixes a real problem. Everything else falls behind. When a CVE fix lands in a major version, you have to jump several majors at once. Version updates, weekly, grouped Small regular steps. Old dependencies don't pile up. A PR every week to review and merge. Needs CI you trust. Version updates, one PR per package Easy to find which bump broke the build. Lots of PRs. Most people stop reading them.

Recommendation

Security updates on everywhere. Version updates weekly and grouped for repos that have CI, and always for github-actions, since actions run with access to your secrets.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Private repos

Secret scanning, push protection and code scanning are free on public repos only. On private repos they need an organization on GitHub Team or Enterprise with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security. Dependabot works on every plan.

Push protection can be bypassed

Anyone with write access can push anyway by picking a reason: It's used in tests, It's a false positive or I'll fix it later. A secret that has been pushed is leaked: revoke it, don't just delete the commit.

Push protection for users

Separate from the repo setting, GitHub blocks pushes of secrets by you to any public repo. It is on by default in your personal settings. Keep it on.
